div.head: Chapter 5
div.p: What was said above is confirmed by a most reasonable law, which makes mention of the people of Persia and of the kingdom and king of the Persians. By this law Romans are forbidden to go and trade there, lest it be suspected that the Roman people wished, under the guise of commerce, to spy out foreign kingdoms: "so that they may not pry into the secrets of another kingdom, which is not fitting," it says there, 4, mercatores, Codex, De commerciis et mercatoribus. Where the emperors Theodosius and Honorius confess that the kingdom of the Persians is foreign to the Roman people.

I do not wish to omit what Bartolus notes in L. christianis, Codex, De paganis et templis eorum: that war ought not to be waged against the Moors unless they had usurped the Holy Land, nor against the Turks unless they impeded the passage of Christians who went with an army to recover it: "Since they contend in something turbulent and contrary to right, because they do not permit us to go to them, therefore the Church declares war upon them; otherwise it would not declare it." These are his words. It appears from them that in the time of Bartolus the Turks did not yet have as much power or as much malice as now to persecute the Christian people.

So if we must be peaceable with the Moors and with the Turks, we have nothing to do with them for good or ill: beyond loving them and desiring their salvation, and insofar as we are able endeavoring to secure it, provided they do not harm the universal Church or do something against us contrary to right; much less do we have anything to do with the other peoples we placed in this fourth category, peaceful ones who have done us no harm, dwelling in their own and most remote regions and kingdoms, far apart from ours, beyond, as I said, loving them and endeavoring to save them.

Of this fourth category of unbelievers, more clearly and distinctly than all others, spoke Cardinal Cajetan on 2.2 q. 66, a. 8, of which he says in particular the following: "There are some unbelievers who are subject neither in law nor in fact to the temporal jurisdiction of Christian princes, as would be the case if pagans were found who were never subjects of the Roman Empire, inhabiting lands in which the Christian name has never been known; for the rulers of these peoples, though unbelievers, are nonetheless legitimate rulers, whether they be governed by royal or by political rule. Nor are they deprived of their rulership on account of unbelief, since rulership derives from positive law and unbelief from divine law, which does not abrogate positive law. And concerning these I know of no law in temporal matters against them: no king, no emperor, nor the Roman Church may wage war to occupy their lands or to subject them temporally; because there is no cause of just war, since Jesus Christ, King of kings, to whom all power in heaven and on earth has been given, sent to take possession of the world not soldiers of an armed host, but holy preachers, as sheep among wolves. And further: 'Therefore we would sin most gravely if we were to strive to spread the faith of Christ by this path. Nor would we be their legitimate rulers, but would be committing great acts of robbery, and would be bound to make restitution as unjust combatants or occupiers. Good preachers ought to be sent to these peoples who by word and example would convert them to God, and not those who would oppress, despoil, scandalize, and subjugate them.'" Thus far Cajetan. Who, in what he says, shows that he well understands all the qualities that the unbelievers of this fourth kind or category possess, and thus how greatly they differ from the other three kinds.
